events.summary: H1 is the strongest of the four and is well grounded on the pricing-engine side: verified findings F2/F13/F15 place cfg-3120 (greeks_v2 5->100) at 12:04:00Z, ~1 minute before the first anomaly in the 12:05Z bucket; F10 provides direct pricing-engine telemetry tying the fault to GreeksV2 specifically (WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms' from 12:05:21Z, 56 ERRORs 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2', CPU 40%->99-100%); F7/F8/F9/F12 establish the order-service symptom is a propagated client-side 2500ms timeout with flat local CPU, and F3/F16 establish order-service -> pricing-engine as the only shared hop. That is a complete, temporally tight, mechanism-specific chain and it deserves to lead. However, the competitors have not been *contradicted by evidence*, only by inference, and the missing discriminator is cheap and obtainable: no pre-ramp pricing-engine baseline, no rollback/restore observation, no traffic-volume series, and no market-data-service or redis-cache telemetry at all (the blast-radius claim rests on just order-service and pricing-engine). The two changes are 8 minutes apart, so timestamp proximity alone cannot carry the case. I am therefore sending three targeted requests; if the pre-ramp baseline plus rollback response come back as expected, H1 is accept-worthy at ~0.9, and if market-data-service/redis-cache/resource series come back flat, H2-H4 collapse to noise. H1 is also over-claiming in one respect: its own assumption that GreeksV2 is 'materially more expensive... not directly measured before/after' is the single load-bearing unverified hop, and the stated 0.82 already exceeds what a 1-minute-only temporal separation plus an unmeasured cost delta can support.

The 12:03Z bucket already shows the step into saturation (cpu max 98.65, p99 max 2534.9), consistent with the 12:04:00Z cfg-3120 change landing at that bucket boundary.

tasks.objective: Query market-data-service metrics (latency_p99_ms, cpu_pct, request_rate) and redis-cache metrics (hit/miss rate, latency, connection count, evictions, failover/reconnect events) across 11:30-13:00Z; did either deviate in the 12:04-12:05Z window or at 11:56Z? Also check whether api-gateway, portfolio-service or exchange-gateway show an independent step in the 12:05Z bucket, to test the blast-radius claim that only order-service and pricing-engine are affected.
tasks.answer: Neither market-data-service nor redis-cache deviated at 11:56Z or in the 12:04-12:05Z window: market-data-service p99 is flat ~39-40ms across 11:30-13:00Z (no step at the 11:56Z protobuf deploy), and redis-cache hit_ratio (~96%), evictions (~3/min), connections (~310) and CPU (~22%) are all flat. Of the candidate cross-services, api-gateway p99 is also flat (~210ms) through the 12:05Z bucket, so no independent step is seen outside the pricing-engine->order-service path — the blast-radius claim that only order-service and pricing-engine are affected is consistent with the metrics I could retrieve. This weakens H2 (protobuf serialization) and H3 (redis-cache degradation) and leaves H1/H4 as the competing explanations, which my data does not distinguish.

critiques.summary: H1 is the strongest of the four and is well grounded on the pricing-engine side: verified findings F2/F13/F15 place cfg-3120 (greeks_v2 5->100) at 12:04:00Z, ~1 minute before the first anomaly in the 12:05Z bucket; F10 provides direct pricing-engine telemetry tying the fault to GreeksV2 specifically (WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms' from 12:05:21Z, 56 ERRORs 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2', CPU 40%->99-100%); F7/F8/F9/F12 establish the order-service symptom is a propagated client-side 2500ms timeout with flat local CPU, and F3/F16 establish order-service -> pricing-engine as the only shared hop. That is a complete, temporally tight, mechanism-specific chain and it deserves to lead. However, the competitors have not been *contradicted by evidence*, only by inference, and the missing discriminator is cheap and obtainable: no pre-ramp pricing-engine baseline, no rollback/restore observation, no traffic-volume series, and no market-data-service or redis-cache telemetry at all (the blast-radius claim rests on just order-service and pricing-engine). The two changes are 8 minutes apart, so timestamp proximity alone cannot carry the case. I am therefore sending three targeted requests; if the pre-ramp baseline plus rollback response come back as expected, H1 is accept-worthy at ~0.9, and if market-data-service/redis-cache/resource series come back flat, H2-H4 collapse to noise. H1 is also over-claiming in one respect: its own assumption that GreeksV2 is 'materially more expensive... not directly measured before/after' is the single load-bearing unverified hop, and the stated 0.82 already exceeds what a 1-minute-only temporal separation plus an unmeasured cost delta can support.

challenges.issue: The load-bearing hop — that the GreeksV2 path is materially more expensive per quote than v1 — is explicitly flagged as unmeasured in H1's own assumptions. Without a pre-ramp pricing-engine baseline (11:56-12:04Z, i.e. when dep-6111 was already live and greeks_v2 was still 5%) versus post-ramp, the causal step from 'flag ramped' to 'CPU saturated' rests on co-timing plus a WARN line, not on a before/after measurement. Note the baseline 'CPU ~40%' in F10 is drawn from 11:30-12:00Z, which straddles the 11:56Z deploy, so it cannot by itself isolate the flag's effect.

Temporal tightness is weaker than stated. cfg-3120 is at 12:04:00Z; the first priced-engine WARN is 12:05:21Z and the earliest metric bucket boundary is 12:05:00Z. With 300s buckets the ordering cfg-3120 vs. first deviation is not resolvable (acknowledged in GAPS). Meanwhile dep-6111 sits 8-9 min earlier and remains live and un-rolled-back — consistent with either (a) a change that takes ~9 min to manifest under a self-warming path, or (b) a change with a lagged effect. Precedence is inferred, not proven.

H2's two middle hops are marked ASSUMED and it is contradicted only by pricing-engine-side evidence (F10/F15/F11) that shows the fault at pricing-engine, not by any market-data-service evidence. H2 is dismissed on the reporter-deploy's timestamp ordering and on absence of market-data-service WARN/ERROR logs — but that absence came from a logs-only query and no metric was ever fetched for market-data-service (its own GAP says so explicitly). The contradiction is therefore indirect and partly grounded in an incomplete data source.

redis-cache was never queried: no hit/miss rate, latency, connection-count, or failover signal exists in any finding. F16/F17 only establish that it is topologically reachable. H3 is dismissed because it requires spontaneous degradation, but spontaneous Redis degradation (cf. HIST-107, cited in F5/F18) leaves exactly this kind of trace and the trace was not looked for. A single shared-store event could also plausibly produce both the pricing-engine CPU saturation (retry spin) and the order-service timeouts without any config change being causal.

No traffic/request-volume series exists anywhere in the findings, so a market-open-style surge (the exact precedent HIST-113, matched on both service and symptoms) is dismissed purely by assumption. H4 is the only alternative with a same-service, same-symptom historical analogue; if volume stepped at 12:04-12:05Z independently of the flag, H1's attribution to cfg-3120 would be confounded. This is testable in one query.

Blast radius is asserted for at least two services but verified for exactly two, with no check on the other services that share the quote path (api-gateway, portfolio-service, exchange-gateway, ledger-db, kafka — see F4/F17). If any of those show a simultaneous step, the 'config change on pricing-engine' framing is incomplete even if pricing-engine is the epicentre. This is secondary to the discrimination problem but should lower the cap.

Calibration: 0.82 for the top hypothesis with three live competitors and an unmeasured central cost hop is too high, and the automated check flags the same. Additionally, one finding the chain leans on (F16) is logged UNVERIFIED while F17 covers overlapping content — the shared-dependency claim should rest on the verified one only.

evidence_requests.question: For pricing-engine, report cpu_pct and latency_p99_ms at sub-bucket resolution (60s or finer) for 11:50:00-12:10:00Z, and separately the same two metrics for the 11:56:00-12:04:00Z interval (when dep-6111 was already live but flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct was still 5%). Was pricing-engine CPU/latency at its ~40%/~60ms baseline for the full 8 minutes between the market-data-service deploy and the cfg-3120 ramp, or did it step at 11:56Z? Also report a request-volume / request-rate series for pricing-engine and order-service over 11:30-13:00Z so we can see whether quote traffic actually surged at 12:04-12:05Z.
evidence_requests.rationale: This is the decisive discriminator for H1 vs H2 and H4. A flat baseline during 11:56-12:04Z with a step exactly at the 12:04Z ramp proves the flag, not the deploy, is causal and rules out a surge; a step at 11:56Z would move H2 to the top. Volume data is the only way to falsify H4 (HIST-113 analogue) instead of dismissing it by assumption.

evidence_requests.question: Is there any post-12:04Z change in cfg-3120's effective value, a rollback of cfg-3120, or a rollback of dep-6111 anywhere in 12:04-13:59Z, and if so what did pricing-engine cpu_pct/p99 and order-service p99/error_rate do in the following 10 minutes? If no rollback occurred, retrieve the latest available pricing-engine cpu_pct and p99 and order-service error_rate at the end of the window (13:55-13:59Z) to establish whether the incident is still ongoing or self-recovered.
evidence_requests.rationale: A rollback of cfg-3120 that restores CPU and timeouts is direct causal proof for H1; a rollback of dep-6111 that fails to fix anything strongly contradicts H2. Current incident state also matters for the mitigation decision.
